cards.definition_en: A lightweight, isolated package that holds an application together with everything it needs to run, sharing the operating system of the host.
examples: Each service runs in its own container, so updates do not affect the others.
The container starts in a second because it does not boot a whole system.
common_mistakes: Thinking a container contains a full separate operating system: it shares the host kernel.
Storing important data only inside a container that will be deleted.

cards.definition_en: A read-only template, built in layers, from which containers are started.
examples: The pipeline builds a new container image after every change.
A small container image downloads and starts faster.
common_mistakes: Confusing a container image with a running container.
Using the 'latest' tag in production and getting unexpected versions.

cards.definition_en: Automatic management of many containers: starting them, restarting failed ones, scaling and connecting them.
examples: Kubernetes is a popular orchestration platform.
Orchestration restarts a crashed service without human help.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a deployment script that runs one command.
Spelling it 'orchestation'.

cards.definition_en: An automated chain of steps, such as build, test and deploy, that runs whenever code changes.
examples: The pipeline failed at the test stage, so nothing was deployed.
Adding a security scan to the pipeline catches problems early.
common_mistakes: Thinking a pipeline is only a tool for deployment: it also builds and tests.
Ignoring a red pipeline and merging anyway.

cards.definition_en: A practice in which developers merge their changes into the shared code many times a day and every merge is built and tested automatically.
examples: Continuous integration found the broken test within minutes of the merge.
Without continuous integration, problems appear only when releases are assembled.
common_mistakes: Merging once a month and calling it continuous integration.
Mixing it up with continuous delivery, which is about releasing.

cards.definition_en: A practice of keeping software always in a state that can be released, with the release steps automated and the final decision made by people.
examples: With continuous delivery the team can release on any weekday.
Continuous delivery needs a reliable set of automated tests.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with continuous deployment, where every change goes live automatically.
Releasing manually from a developer's laptop.

cards.definition_en: Describing servers, networks and other resources in files kept in version control, so they can be created and changed automatically.
examples: With infrastructure as code a new environment is created from a file in minutes.
Reviewing infrastructure as code changes works like reviewing application code.
common_mistakes: Creating servers by hand and only documenting them afterwards.
Storing passwords in the infrastructure as code files.

cards.definition_en: Creating and preparing resources such as servers, databases or user accounts so that they are ready for use.
examples: Automated provisioning gives every new employee an account on the first day.
Provisioning a test server takes only a few minutes in the cloud.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with deployment, which puts an application on resources that already exist.
Spelling it 'provisionning'.

cards.definition_en: Automatic adding or removing of computing resources according to how busy a system is.
examples: Autoscaling added more servers during the sale and removed them at night.
A wrong autoscaling rule can create a large bill.
common_mistakes: Expecting autoscaling to fix a slow database query.
Setting no upper limit for the number of servers.

cards.definition_en: Continuously collecting and checking numbers about a system, such as load and errors, to know whether it is healthy.
examples: Monitoring showed that memory use grew every hour.
Without monitoring, the team learns about outages from angry customers.
common_mistakes: Watching only whether the server is on and ignoring errors.
Mixing it up with observability, which is about understanding why something happens.

cards.definition_en: How well you can understand what happens inside a system by looking at its logs, metrics and traces.
examples: Good observability helped to find the slow step in the request.
Tracing is an important part of observability for services that call each other.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym of monitoring.
Collecting logs but never connecting them to requests.

cards.definition_en: Recording messages about what an application is doing, so problems can be investigated later.
examples: Centralized logging lets engineers search the logs of all servers in one place.
Never write passwords into logging output.
common_mistakes: Writing sensitive data into logs.
Keeping logs only on the server that fails.

cards.definition_en: Automatically notifying people when a measured value crosses a limit or something goes wrong.
examples: Alerting woke the engineer when the error rate doubled.
Too many alerting rules cause alert fatigue.
common_mistakes: Sending an alert for every small fluctuation.
Sending alerts to a mailbox nobody reads.

cards.definition_en: The duty of being available to respond to incidents outside normal working hours, according to a schedule.
examples: The on-call engineer received an alert at three in the morning.
A fair on-call rotation shares the duty between all team members.
common_mistakes: Writing 'on call' as one word or with a hyphen inconsistently: the noun and adjective use a hyphen, 'on call' is the phrase.
Expecting one person to be on call all the time.

cards.definition_en: The share of time during which a service or computer is working and available.
examples: The provider promises an uptime of 99.9 percent.
Planned maintenance is usually excluded from uptime figures.
common_mistakes: Confusing uptime with speed: a service can be up but slow.
Counting a partly broken service as fully up.

cards.definition_en: A formal promise to a customer about the quality of a service, for example how much of the time it will be available.
examples: The service level agreement guarantees that the system is available 99.9 percent of the time.
The customer received a refund because of a broken service level agreement.
common_mistakes: Treating the promised number as the real result.
Confusing an agreement with a customer and an internal target.

cards.definition_en: A release method with two identical environments: the new version is prepared in the idle one and traffic is switched to it all at once.
examples: With a blue-green deployment the old version stays ready for a quick return.
Switching traffic in a blue-green deployment takes seconds.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a canary release, where traffic moves gradually.
Forgetting that both environments need the same database changes.

cards.definition_en: A way of publishing a new version to a small group of users first and to everyone only if no problems appear.
examples: A canary release sent the new version to five percent of the users.
The team stopped the canary release when errors increased.
common_mistakes: Releasing to the whole user base and calling it a canary.
Not watching metrics during the canary phase.

cards.definition_en: A setting that turns a feature on or off without releasing new code.
examples: A feature flag let the team switch off the broken search in seconds.
Old feature flags should be removed from the code.
common_mistakes: Leaving old feature flags in the code for years.
Hiding a security fix behind a flag that nobody enables.

cards.definition_en: An environment that copies the production system as closely as possible, used for final checks before release.
examples: The change worked in staging, but production had different data.
Staging should use the same configuration as production, but not real customer data.
common_mistakes: Using real customer data in staging without protection.
Confusing staging with the developer's laptop.

cards.definition_en: Safely storing, handing out and renewing passwords, keys and tokens so they are not kept in code or in plain files.
examples: Secrets management keeps database passwords out of the repository.
The vault issues short-lived credentials as part of secrets management.
common_mistakes: Committing a key to the repository 'just for now'.
Using the same secret for development and production.

cards.definition_en: A software imitation of a whole computer, with its own operating system, running on a physical machine.
examples: Each customer receives a separate virtual machine in the cloud.
A virtual machine takes longer to start than a container.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with a container, which shares the host kernel.
Thinking a virtual machine uses no real resources.

cards.definition_en: A cloud model in which the provider runs your code on demand and manages the servers, and you pay only for the time it runs.
examples: A serverless function resizes the picture each time a user uploads one.
Serverless can be cheap for rare tasks and costly for constant load.
common_mistakes: Believing there are no servers at all: they exist, but you do not manage them.
Expecting no delay when a rarely used function starts.

cards.definition_en: A separate data centre location inside a cloud region, with its own power and network, used to survive local failures.
examples: The database is replicated across two availability zones.
When one availability zone failed, the service stayed online.
common_mistakes: Putting all servers into one availability zone.
Confusing an availability zone with a region, which contains several zones.

cards.definition_en: Gradual differences between the real settings of servers and their intended settings, caused by manual changes.
examples: Manual fixes on one server caused configuration drift, and the next release failed there.
Infrastructure as code helps to reduce configuration drift.
common_mistakes: Changing settings by hand on production servers.
Thinking the drift is a software bug and not a process problem.
